title: Two-length builders
pages: With unlimited copies of two positive integer rod lengths a and b, a target n is reachable exactly when n = ax + by for nonnegative integers x, y. Rod order does not matter; cutting, overlaps, and negative rods are forbidden.

Finite evidence can certify infinitely many targets. If a consecutive integers N, ..., N+a-1 are reachable, then every integer at least N is reachable: repeatedly add an a-rod to these a starting builds.

Exact boundary. If gcd(a,b)=1 and a,b>1, the largest impossible target is ab-a-b, so every target at least (a-1)(b-1) works. If gcd(a,b)>1, every target not divisible by that gcd is impossible, giving infinitely many gaps. A 1-rod makes every nonnegative target possible, so there is no largest positive gap in that case.

K-1: Investigate small builds, distinguish rearranging from a new combination, and physically continue a run. Counting and alignment to 18 are enough; adults can record. A repeated construction is a genuine explanation without the formula.

Grades 2-3: Make exhaustive small lists, then find a short certificate for no later gaps. Addition to 28 and willingness to organize cases help. The shared-factor example refutes an overbroad conjecture.

Grades 4-5: Explain completeness, compare last gaps, conjecture the formula, and justify eventual coverage for a chosen coprime pair. Multiplication and remainders support the last questions; the general formula proof is adult backup.

For the current ten children, use five pair-kits: ten copies each of rods 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7 on one unit scale, plus graph-paper strips and scissors for invented lengths. Existing measured rods or cut paper strips both work. Use the printed ruler scale when placing rods directly on a worksheet; otherwise build beside it on matching graph paper. Give each pair a pencil and a few target cards. Reuse rods between targets; large targets can be represented by counts.
Print only the starting pages and keep later problems available. The aim is a convincing construction or obstruction, not completion of all three packets.

0-5 minutes: Let pairs handle rods, then build 7 from 3 and 4 beside the shared student example. Align at zero. Show that reversing the rods reaches the same target and is the same combination; a gap or overhang is not a build.

5-22: Choose K P1-2, 2-3 P1-3, or 4-5 P1-2. 22-27: Stand up and carry one successful target and one doubtful target to another pair. 27-48: Stay with the investigation or offer K P4-6, 2-3 P4-6, or upper P3-8. 48-60: Share one claim and the build or obstruction that establishes it. Leave the general formula as a conjecture if proof is not yet within reach.
P1. Of the listed targets, 6=3+3, 8=4+4, 9=3+3+3, 10=3+3+4 work. The targets 1, 2, 5 do not. One rod is too long for 1 or 2; for 5, one rod is too short and two rods total at least 6.
P2. For 12: four 3-rods or three 4-rods. For 15: five 3-rods, or one 3-rod and three 4-rods. These are all: after choosing the number of 4-rods, the remainder must be a multiple of 3.
P3. With 3 and 5, 4 and 7 are impossible. The others work: 8=3+5, 9=3+3+3, 10=5+5, 11=3+3+5, 12=3+3+3+3. For 7, no 5 leaves a multiple of 3: the possible remainders are 7 and 2.
P4. Start with 6=3+3, 7=3+4, 8=4+4; add 3 to reach 9,10,11, then 12,13,14, then 15,16,17, then 18. These three chains keep going forever and cover every integer at least 6.
P5. Exactly 2,4,6,8,10,12 work. Both rods are made of whole pairs of units; joining them always leaves an even length. Every positive even length is made from 2-rods.

P6. Exactly {2,3}, {2,5}, {3,4} cover every target 6-12. For {2,3}, use 2-rods for even targets and one 3 plus 2-rods for odd targets. For {2,5}, do the same with one 5 for odd targets. The failures are {2,4}: 7; {3,5}: 7; {4,5}: 6,7,11. This checks all six distinct pairs.

For an “all ways” task, ask what happens with zero, one, two, ... of the longer rod. For an infinite claim, put three adjacent 3/4 builds side by side and ask whether each can grow. For an impossibility claim, ask for the full short list of possible longer-rod counts.
P1. In 1-16, only 1,2,5 fail. The certificate 6,7,8 plus added 3-rods covers all later targets.

P2. Writing (number of 3-rods, number of 4-rods): 12 has (4,0),(0,3); 16 has (4,1),(0,4); 24 has (8,0),(4,3),(0,6). The number of 4-rods has one required remainder modulo 3, so stepping by three 4-rods lists every possibility.
P3. The impossible lengths in 1-20 are 1,2,4,7. The last is 7: 8=3+5, 9=3+3+3, 10=5+5, followed by added 3-rods, settle all later targets.
P4. Minimal consecutive certificates are 6,7,8 for 3/4 and 8,9,10 for 3/5. Any other finite collection that demonstrably covers every remainder and starts beyond the last gap is acceptable.
P5. Last gap 17. A certificate is 18=4+7+7, 19=4+4+4+7, 20=4+4+4+4+4, 21=7+7+7; then add 4-rods. For 17, using zero, one or two 7-rods leaves 17,10 or 3; none is divisible by 4.
P6. The claim is false: 2/4 misses every odd length. The pair 4/7 does eventually have no gaps, as P5 proves. One counterexample is enough to refute “every pair.”
P1. Exactly 1,2,5. Check these small failures and use the three-build certificate above; a long tested list alone does not prove completeness.

P2. Last gaps: 3/5 → 7; 4/5 → 11; 4/7 → 17. Certificates: 8,9,10 as above; 12=4+4+4, 13=4+4+5, 14=4+5+5, 15=5+5+5; and 18,19,20,21 as above. For gap 11 with 4/5, zero, one, two 5-rods leave 11,6,1, none divisible by 4.
P3-4. All twelve targets 18-29 work: use the four builds 18-21 and add 4 once or twice. Target 17 fails by the three-case argument above.

P5. 2/4, 3/6 and 4/6 have infinitely many gaps (odd targets, nonmultiples of 3, and odd targets respectively). The pairs 3/5 and 4/7 have only finitely many. The dividing line is a common divisor greater than 1; the coprime direction needs the argument on the next page.
P6. All ways for 24 are (8,0),(4,3),(0,6). Replace four 3-rods by three 4-rods, or reverse that replacement. Equality of two builds gives 3Δx=-4Δy, forcing changes to be multiples of this exchange.

P7. Last gap for 5/7 is 23. It is impossible because zero to three 7-rods leave 23,16,9,2, none divisible by 5. A certificate is 24=5+5+7+7, 25=5×5, 26=5+7+7+7, 27=5+5+5+5+7, 28=7×4. Adding 5 covers all later targets. The earlier last gaps 5,7,11,17 and this 23 fit ab-a-b. These examples support a conjecture, not a proof of the formula.

P8. Many choices work. Example: 2/5 has builds 4 and 5, so all targets at least 4 work. In general, assume a,b are positive and coprime. The a numbers 0,b,2b,...,(a-1)b have different remainders modulo a: equal remainders would make a divide (j-k)b and hence j-k, impossible for distinct indices in 0,...,a-1. Each remainder therefore has a reachable starting value; add a-rods within each remainder class. This proves eventual coverage for any invented pair. If a=1, the conclusion is immediate.
Why the exact last-gap formula holds

For a,b>1 coprime, set F=ab-a-b. If F=ax+by with x,y≥0, then a(x+1)+b(y+1)=ab. Reducing modulo b shows b divides x+1. Since x+1>0, the first term is at least ab, and the second term is positive: contradiction.

For N≥F+1, choose j in {0,...,a-1} so that jb and N have the same remainder modulo a. Then N-jb is a multiple of a and N-jb≥1-a. A multiple of a strictly greater than -a must be nonnegative, so N=ai+jb with i≥0. Thus F is impossible and every larger integer is possible.

For children, a small complete certificate is usually a better endpoint than this symbolic proof. Ask a child who says “it always works” to identify whether they have tested a range, found a repeatable construction, or proved the general statement.

If a group owns the coverage idea, ask for two rod pairs with the same last gap and a certificate for each: 2/7 and 3/4 both have last gap 5. This tests whether the boundary determines the pieces. Stop before turning the session into a large search table.
This is a new rod-reachability investigation in the current library, rather than a claim that divisibility itself is new to returning children. All grade adaptations here are unpiloted.

Dilip Barman, Chapel Hill Math Circle, “The Frobenius Coin Problem,” Beginners’ Group (grades 1-3), 18 January 2025, pp. 1-4. Direct precedent for the coin-reachability question and a finite pattern of builds establishing eventual coverage.
